chief_complaint: recurrent skin abscesses and a new large mass in his liver
hpi_details: 12-year-old male presents with right upper quadrant abdominal pain and fever. Ultrasound reveals a large liver abscess. His past medical history is significant for multiple recurrent severe skin abscesses requiring surgical drainage, and a previous hospitalization for Aspergillus pneumonia. He has a history of swollen, suppurative lymph nodes.
ideas: thinks he just has bad luck with staph infections
concerns: worried about having to undergo another surgery for the liver mass
expectations: wants antibiotics to cure the liver infection without surgery
pmh: Recurrent Staphylococcal skin abscesses, Aspergillus pneumonia, lymphadenitis

available_results.value: 8.2 cm complex collection in the right hepatic lobe, consistent with a liver abscess

core_concepts: CGD is a defect in the phagocyte NADPH oxidase complex, preventing neutrophils from generating the oxidative burst needed to kill catalase-positive organisms.
Catalase-positive organisms (Staphylococcus aureus, Burkholderia cepacia, Serratia marcescens, Nocardia, Aspergillus) cause recurrent severe infections (abscesses, pneumonias, osteomyelitis).
Granuloma formation can lead to obstructive symptoms (e.g., GI or GU tract obstruction).
Diagnosis involves the Dihydrorhodamine (DHR) 123 flow cytometry test or Nitroblue tetrazolium (NBT) test.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: recurrent skin abscesses and a new large mass in his liver
Key HPI features: Recurrent deep tissue abscesses (skin, liver) and fungal pneumonia (Aspergillus).
Objective/Exam findings: Tender hepatomegaly, scars from previous abscess drainages.
common_misconceptions: Assuming recurrent abscesses are just MRSA colonization without considering an underlying immune defect in deep/visceral abscesses.
dangerous_errors: Failing to cover for fungal organisms (Aspergillus) in a patient with CGD presenting with pneumonia.
Not referring siblings for genetic testing.
management_principles: Lifelong prophylaxis with Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (bacterial) and Itraconazole (fungal).
Interferon-gamma therapy to augment phagocyte antimicrobial activity in some cases.
Aggressive early treatment of infections, often requiring surgical drainage.
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 12-year-old male with history of recurrent severe skin abscesses and Aspergillus pneumonia presents with fever and RUQ pain. Ultrasound shows liver abscess.
reference_soap.objective: T 38.8C. RUQ tenderness. Multiple surgical scars on skin. DHR flow cytometry confirms absent oxidative burst.
reference_soap.assessment: Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) with acute liver abscess (likely S. aureus).
reference_soap.plan: 1. Admit and begin empiric IV antimicrobial therapy in consultation with Infectious Diseases, then tailor treatment to abscess cultures and susceptibilities. 2. Interventional radiology consult for abscess drainage and culture. 3. Initiate lifelong Bactrim and Itraconazole prophylaxis after acute-treatment planning. 4. Genetic counseling.

learning_objectives: Identify the susceptibility to catalase-positive organisms (Staph, Aspergillus, Burkholderia) in CGD
Recognize deep tissue and visceral abscesses as hallmark signs
Understand the DHR test and the need for continuous antimicrobial prophylaxis

teaching.one_liner: A phagocyte defect causing inability to kill specific bacteria and fungi, leading to recurrent severe skin and organ abscesses.
differentials: Cystic Fibrosis (if presenting with lung infections)
red_flags: Liver or deep organ abscesses in a child
Infection with unusual organisms like Burkholderia cepacia or Nocardia

must_ask.objective: Identify the pattern of deep infections
must_ask.say: Have you ever had infections deep inside your body, like in your liver, bones, or lungs, before this?
Were you ever told you had a fungal or mold infection in your lungs?
Have you ever had problems with food getting stuck or trouble urinating due to blockages?

history.answer: He has been running a high fever and complaining of constant pain in the upper right side of his belly for the past four days.
His fever started four days ago on Thursday and has remained high without breaking.
The fever stays around thirty-nine degrees day and night, and he has had severe shivering episodes.
We gave him children's ibuprofen and acetaminophen, but they only drop his fever slightly for an hour before it spikes back up.
He has no cough, phlegm, runny nose, sore throat, or trouble catching his breath right now.
He has no burning when he urinates, does not need to go more frequently, and has no back or flank pain.
It is a steady, throbbing ache under his right ribs that hurts more if he moves, but he has had no vomiting or loose stools.
He has a mild headache from the high temperature, but his neck is not stiff and he knows exactly where he is.
We have not seen any skin rash, dark bug bite scabs, or joint swelling anywhere on his body.
He wakes up soaked in sweat every night, and he has lost around two kilograms over the past few weeks because of low appetite.
He has had swollen lymph nodes in his neck and armpits that filled with pus before, but none are red or draining right now.
We have not traveled outside the city, he has not gone camping or hiking in tall grass, and we do not keep any pets.
Nobody else at home or in his middle school class has had a fever or similar illness recently.
He has never received chemotherapy, steroids, or any medicines that weaken his immune system.
He has never had any heart murmurs or heart conditions, and he has not had any dental procedures recently.
He has not started taking any new prescription pills or over-the-counter supplements.
He is only twelve years old, so he is not sexually active and has never used needles or recreational drugs.
He is quite tired and stays in bed most of the day, but he drinks fluids, urinates regularly, and has never had a seizure.
Ever since he was small, he has had deep, painful skin boils and abscesses that required surgeons to cut them open and drain them.
Two years ago he had to stay in the hospital for three weeks with a severe lung infection caused by a fungus called Aspergillus.
He has never had food getting stuck when swallowing, nor has he had any blockages in his bowels or bladder.
He thinks he just has terrible luck and keeps picking up nasty staph bacteria everywhere.
He is very afraid of going into surgery again and having another operation to cut open his liver.
We are really hoping strong antibiotics can clear up this liver infection so he will not need another surgery.
His main health issues have been recurrent staph skin abscesses, the fungal pneumonia episode, and infected lymph nodes.
He has had multiple hospital visits for skin abscess drainage procedures and one long admission for his fungal lung infection.
He does not take any daily maintenance medications right now.
He has no known allergies to any medicines or foods.
Nobody smokes around him at home, and he does not smoke or vape.
He does not drink any alcohol.
He is a seventh grader living at home with both of his parents.
His maternal uncle passed away as a young child from a severe infection, but both parents are healthy.
He was born full-term with a normal delivery and had no newborn complications.
He reached all milestones normally, though his weight gain has been a bit slow lately.
He has received all his standard childhood immunizations on schedule without any bad reactions.
He attends middle school in person, and there are no outbreaks of infections reported in his class.

exam.finding: Temperature 38.8°C, blood pressure 108/70 mmHg, pulse 108 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, oxygen saturation 98% on room air.
The patient appears acutely ill, flushed, and uncomfortable, holding his right upper abdomen.
Oropharynx is clear without tonsillar enlargement, exudates, or mucosal lesions; mucous membranes are moist.
Both tympanic membranes are intact and pearly gray with normal light reflexes and no erythema.
Multiple firm, mobile, non-tender cervical lymph nodes are palpable bilaterally with healed overlying surgical scars.
Lungs are clear to auscultation bilaterally with normal vesicular breath sounds and no wheezes or crackles.
Regular tachycardia with normal first and second heart sounds; no murmurs, gallops, or friction rubs.
Abdomen is flat and symmetric without distension, visible pulsations, or surgical scars.
Marked focal tenderness to palpation in the right upper quadrant with voluntary guarding but no rigidity.
No rebound tenderness elicited in the right upper quadrant or elsewhere across the abdomen.
Tender hepatomegaly with the liver edge palpated 3 cm below the right costal margin; spleen is not palpable.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion bilaterally.
Multiple well-healed linear surgical scars across the axillae, neck, and back from prior drainage; no active boils, rashes, or petechiae.
Neck is supple with full passive flexion; Kernig and Brudzinski signs are negative.
